oil.summary: Crude posted another strong session, with Brent clearing $94/bbl (+2.59%) and WTI at $86.84 (+1.15%), extending a near-8% weekly rally in Brent as Middle East risk premiums remain firmly bid. The US-Iran impasse is the dominant driver: Tehran is holding the Strait of Hormuz closed pending deal terms, Chinese state tankers are rerouting away from both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and Iranian crude is described as effectively locked out of global markets. Supply routes are fracturing further, pushing supertanker rates to record highs. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone strikes continue to hammer Russian refining capacity — including a fresh hit on an oil terminal in Krasnodar Krai today — fuelling a domestic fuel rationing crisis in Russia. Chinese refiners are scrambling for alternative barrels, snapping up 8 million barrels of Iraqi Basrah grades for prompt delivery. RBOB gasoline's sharp -7.79% drop and heating oil's -2.35% dip suggest product-specific demand or crack dynamics, with diesel cracks separately reported near $100 — pointing to a tighter underlying market than headline crude levels imply. SLB's preparation to restart 15 rigs in Venezuela is a modest supply-side offset to watch.
drivers: US-Iran standoff: Strait of Hormuz remains closed, Iranian barrels effectively off the market, pushing Brent to three-week highs
Ukrainian drone campaign intensifies against Russian refining infrastructure, spreading domestic fuel rationing inside Russia
Chinese refiners pivot to Iraqi crude amid Gulf route disruptions; supertanker rates hit all-time highs on Middle East demand surge

gas.summary: The gas picture today is a stark transatlantic divergence. Henry Hub slipped -1.81% to $2.763/MMBtu, remaining under pressure on a one-month basis (-5.54%), suggesting ample domestic US supply conditions. TTF, by contrast, surged +2.71% to €65.1/MWh, building on a near +8% weekly gain, as the Hormuz closure and an extended LNG squeeze erode European supply confidence. The sole headline in our feed signals that market optimism around a diplomatic resolution has faded materially, with traders now positioning for a prolonged oil and LNG supply crunch. News flow for this sector is thin beyond that single forward-looking note; traders should weight TTF's move primarily against the broader Middle East supply disruption narrative visible in oil headlines.
drivers: TTF +2.71% on the week, driven by fading hopes for a US-Iran deal and an anticipated extended LNG supply squeeze into Europe
Henry Hub continues to lag, down -5.54% on the month, reflecting divergent US domestic supply conditions
News flow is limited today; TTF price action is best read as a spillover from the Hormuz closure and broader Middle East risk premium

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up modestly to $78.00/EUA (+0.77%), though the market remains marginally soft on a one-month basis (-0.95%). TTF's continued climb (+2.71% today) raises gas-to-power switching costs, creating mild upward pressure on carbon as coal-backed generation becomes relatively more competitive — consistent with the headline reaffirming coal's dominant global power generation share despite accelerating renewables buildout. Geopolitical noise adds complexity: Ukraine is pushing the EU to sanction Rosatom following reported safety failures, which could disrupt nuclear supply chains in Central Europe. A separate blackout traced to a Kyrgyz hydropower plant underscores fragility in Central Asian grids. Iran's Hormuz closure, flagged in this sector's feed as well, carries indirect implications for LNG-dependent power generation across Asia and Southern Europe. Overall, headline data for this sector is moderate; the carbon price itself remains range-bound.
drivers: Rising TTF (+2.71%) increases gas-to-power costs, supporting coal's competitive position and applying mild upward pressure to EUAs
Ukraine's push to sanction Rosatom introduces nuclear supply chain risk for EU member states dependent on Russian fuel assemblies
Central Asia blackout traced to hydropower failure highlights grid fragility; Hormuz closure poses indirect risk to LNG-fed power markets
